summary: Provides the protocol mechanisms for using ECC Brainpool curves with TLS 1.3. These curves were options in TLS 1.2, were dropped for TLS 1.3 because of little use, and have not been shown to be significantly weak, so some people still want them.

eli5.summary: Some special math shapes used for secret handshakes were removed from the newest version of the web's lock. This lets people put several of them back.

questions: how to use brainpool curves in tls 1.3
why were brainpool curves removed from tls 1.3
subtitle: Support for ECC Brainpool cryptographic curves in the latest TLS version

tldr.problem: TLS 1.3 dropped support for ECC Brainpool curves that were used in TLS 1.2 due to limited deployment, but these curves have not been proven cryptographically weak and some users still want to use them.
tldr.mechanism: This RFC defines how to negotiate and use three ECC Brainpool curves (256-bit, 384-bit, and 512-bit variants) in TLS 1.3 by assigning new NamedGroup and SignatureScheme identifiers.
tldr.outcome: Implementers who need Brainpool curve support in TLS 1.3 can now use these curves, though the IETF does not endorse this approach and recommends using the natively supported curves instead.

today: RFC 8734 is an Informational document published in February 2020 and has not been obsoleted. It is not an Internet Standard and represents the independent work of its authors. Users who need Brainpool curve support in TLS 1.3 can implement according to this RFC, but should be aware that the IETF recommends the natively supported curves in TLS 1.3.

sections.title: Introduction
sections.content:
The ECC Brainpool curves are a set of elliptic curve groups defined in RFC 5639 for use in cryptographic applications. These curves were generated in a verifiably pseudorandom way and comply with security requirements from international standards.

RFC 8422 and RFC 7027 defined how to use these curves for authentication and key exchange in TLS 1.2 and earlier versions. However, TLS 1.3 (defined in RFC 8446) deprecated the Brainpool curve identifiers due to lack of widespread deployment. This RFC provides the necessary protocol mechanisms to use three ECC Brainpool curves in TLS 1.3 for those who need them, while noting that this approach is not endorsed by the IETF.
sections.eli5: Different organizations created special math shapes to secure connections. Some of them were used in the old lock system but not many people needed them. Here is how to use some of those shapes in the new lock system.

sections.title: Brainpool Curves and Their Use
sections.content:
The RFC specifies three Brainpool curves: brainpoolP256r1, brainpoolP384r1, and brainpoolP512r1, corresponding to 256-bit, 384-bit, and 512-bit key sizes. Each curve is assigned a NamedGroup identifier (values 31, 32, and 33) for use in the TLS supported_groups extension during handshake negotiation.

For signature authentication, the RFC defines three corresponding SignatureScheme values that pair each Brainpool curve with a specific hash function: SHA-256 for the 256-bit curve, SHA-384 for the 384-bit curve, and SHA-512 for the 512-bit curve. The RFC emphasizes that implementers should understand the strengths and weaknesses of all cryptographic mechanisms they use.
sections.eli5: The three shapes come in small, medium, and large sizes. Each one has a number so software can recognize it. When you sign something, you also pick which checking number to use with each shape.

sections.title: Security Requirements
sections.content:
When using Brainpool curves for key exchange with ECDHE (Elliptic Curve Diffie-Hellman Ephemeral), implementations MUST validate each peer's public value by ensuring it is a valid point on the elliptic curve. Failure to conduct this check allows attackers to force the key exchange into a small subgroup where the shared secret can be guessed with far less effort.

The RFC also warns that elliptic curve cryptography implementations may be susceptible to side-channel attacks. Implementations that use twisted curve representations for efficient arithmetic should take particular care to protect against such attacks. Overall cryptographic strength depends on choosing commensurate strengths across key derivation, symmetric encryption, and signature algorithms, following recommendations from standards organizations.
sections.eli5: When two computers agree on a secret using these shapes, they must check that each other's numbers are really on the shape. Secret computation can leak information if the computer is careless, so care is needed.

sections.title: IANA Registry Updates
sections.content: IANA has registered the three Brainpool curves in the TLS Supported Groups registry and the corresponding signature scheme values in the TLS SignatureScheme registry. The curves are marked as not recommended for new deployments, reflecting the IETF's preference for the curves natively supported in TLS 1.3. The registrations include explicit references to this RFC so implementers can understand the context and limitations of these curves.
sections.eli5: The official registry of TLS shapes now includes entries for these three Brainpool shapes, but marks them as not recommended for new uses.

sections.title: Use of Existing ECDHE Encoding
sections.content: The RFC reuses the existing ECDHE parameter encoding defined in TLS 1.3 for the Brainpool curves, rather than defining new encoding schemes. This means that the serialization and deserialization of curve points follows the same conventions used for the natively supported curves in TLS 1.3, simplifying implementation and reducing the risk of encoding errors.
sections.eli5: The computer code that reads and writes these numbers uses the same format as the newer shapes already in TLS 1.3, so less new code is needed.
